title: The wolf and the lamb (Isaiah 11:1–9)
hookLine: a shoot from a stump, and a little child will lead them

lines: A GREEN SHOOT FROM THE SIDE.
cards: A forest a few years after the loggers have gone: stumps everywhere, flat, gray, finished. But look closer. Out of the side of an old stump, a thin green shoot with two or three leaves.
The tree was cut down. The roots weren't. Isaiah had watched the royal family of David shrink and fail: kings who trusted armies instead of God, a kingdom being cut down to the ground.
And from that stump, he saw something growing.

teach.h: A ROD OUT OF THE STEM OF JESSE.
teach.b: In the King James Bible: "And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots." Jesse was David's father.
Some readers hear in that a return past David, to the roots, before the kings went wrong.
On this new shoot, Isaiah says, the spirit of the Lord will rest: wisdom, understanding, counsel, might, knowledge, the fear of the Lord.

teach.h: A KING WHO JUDGES THE POOR FAIRLY.
teach.b: This king won't judge by what his eyes see or his ears hear. He'll judge the poor with fairness.

Then the picture everyone remembers: "The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid; and the calf and the young lion and the fatling together; and a little child shall lead them."
Every pair is a predator and its dinner. A baby plays at the hole of a snake. The world's whole food chain, the logic of eat or be eaten, stops.

teach.h: A LITTLE CHILD SHALL LEAD THEM.
teach.b: A little child, leading. One slip worth catching: people sometimes quote it as the lion shall lie down with the lamb. The text never says that.
It's the wolf that dwells with the lamb, the leopard that lies down with the kid. The vision ends: "They shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain."
Christians read the shoot of Jesse as Jesus, and some churches hang a Jesse tree in Advent, tracing his family. Jewish tradition reads it as the hope of a messiah still to come.
Both keep the picture of a world where nothing preys on anything.

how: Isaiah 11 is often read during Advent, and some families and congregations make a Jesse tree, hanging ornaments for the stories of Jesus's ancestors; the Quaker painter Edward Hicks painted this vision as The Peaceable Kingdom.

o: a new shoot from Jesse's stump, a coming king
a side road leading off the way to Jerusalem
a family of priests who served in the Temple

games.q: what's inside the vision — tap the pairs.

s: Isaiah says the lion shall lie down with the lamb
the text says the wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard lie down with the kid.
the shoot grows from Jesse, David's father
the new shoot comes from the family's roots, before David was king.
the new king judges by what he sees and hears
he won't judge by his eyes or ears, but with fairness for the poor.

games.q: the royal tree of David has been cut down to a stump. what does Isaiah see next?
o: a green shoot growing from its roots.
a new tree planted somewhere else.
games.why: "there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse." hope grows from the roots of what was cut down.

practice: Think of something in your life that feels cut down, a friendship that ended, a plan that failed, a part of you that went quiet, and picture it as a stump.
Then look closely, the way you would in a forest, for a small green shoot: a new habit, a reconnection, a lesson, a beginning you hadn't noticed.
Let your attention rest on it without demanding it be a tree yet, and if you pray, give thanks for it.

wordCard.voice: Branch. The shoot Isaiah sees growing from the stump of Jesse, bringing a peace where the wolf lives with the lamb.

orig.note: Hebrew: a shoot from the stump of Jesse. geza is a cut-down trunk.
